findings.claim: `definite?: boolean | undefined` creates an ambiguous three-state flag (true/false/absent) whose absent case has no defined meaning, so producers that forget to set it may be read as "definite" by some consumers and "not definite" by others.
findings.rationale: The doc comment only specifies what `false` means. Because the property is optional, omission is the default for every producer, and `if (fn.definite)` vs `if (fn.definite !== false)` give opposite answers for an unset flag. If the intended default is "definite", the safe encoding would be a required boolean or an inverted explicitly-set flag so omission fails conservatively. Fairly confident this is a real ambiguity, though the correct default depends on consumer code not shown in this hunk.

findings.claim: Storing `definite` as a property on the function object means it is silently dropped whenever a compiled fn is wrapped in another function, causing the wrapper to read as `undefined`.
findings.rationale: Same hazard already exists for `code`. Any memoization, async-fallback, or re-export site that returns `(input) => inner(input)` loses the flag, and combined with the ambiguous default this could yield an incorrect soundness decision. Low-to-moderate confidence since I cannot see whether such wrapping sites exist in this file.

findings.claim: `code` and the new `definite` are not `readonly`, so callers can mutate the soundness flag on a compiled function after creation.
findings.rationale: A mutable public flag that encodes a correctness invariant can be flipped by any holder of the function. Marking both `readonly` has no runtime cost. Confident this is a safety improvement, though it is not an active bug.
